# Closing the two open decisions: citations are what the answer cited (scoring-spec v2.2), and Perplexity's `Retry-After` is honoured once

**2026-09-12.** Both were measured and proposed in earlier entries and
left for a decision; this entry implements them. **Real spend: ten
Perplexity calls, under five cents.**

## Citations, v2.2 — implemented as proposed

`ClaudeSearchAdapter` now sends `allowed_callers: ["direct"]`, the only
path on which the answer's own `web_search_result_location` citations
come back (the "what a citation is" entry: none in fifteen filtered
responses, 7.5 an answer on direct). `_extract_citations` reads those
first and falls back to the retrieved `web_search_tool_result` blocks only
when the answer cited nothing inline — `_read_agent_output`'s rule for
Perplexity, so the two engines' rows now mean one thing. The adapter's
version is `claude-opus-5/web_search_20260209/direct`: the tool version
did not change, but what a row means did, so the suffix is the provenance
a reader of old rows needs — a `claude_search` row without it holds every
result retrieved. **The 5,277 stored rows across 23 scans are not
rewritten**, per rule 5; `scoring-spec.md` carries the `v2.2` changelog
line and a body paragraph stating the definition, and the `Citation`
model's docstring says the same. Measured cost of the direct path, from
the earlier entry: 7.7% cheaper and half the tail latency at twelve
prompts, twice. `tests/test_claude_citations.py` pins the request shape,
the cited-first rule, the fallback, and that none of the three readers
touches publisher copy. The engine is not a default since this morning,
so no customer sees this until a scan names it — fixed now anyway, while
the measurement and the context both hold.

## `Retry-After`, honoured once — the fix Epic 21.1 deferred

On a 429, `PerplexityAdapter.ask` now reads the vendor's `Retry-After`,
and if it names a wait that still leaves room for one more attempt inside
`ENGINE_CALL_CEILING` — at most 32s, `PERPLEXITY_RETRY_AFTER_MAX` — sleeps
it, **re-enters the start pacer**, and tries once more. A 429 with no
wait, a wait too long, or a second 429 is recorded as
`PROVIDER_RATE_LIMITED` exactly as before; refused requests are unbilled,
so the retry is free. Both 429 kinds Epic 21.1 saw fit: the entry bucket's
`Retry-After: 1` and the 11–17s overload waits.

**Probed against the real account** (`scripts/verify_perplexity_retry.py`),
the way the pacer itself was verified:

| | 429s | answered |
|---|---|---|
| five starts together, pacer bypassed (the shape that drew 429s in Epic 21.1) | **4**, each `Retry-After: 1`, each retried once | **5 / 5** |
| five through `ask_all` — pacer and gate, the production path | 0 | 5 / 5 |

The retries in part 1 came back 1.5s to 6.5s after the start, spaced by
the pacer they re-entered rather than fired together, and part 2 shows
the pacer alone still prevents the bucket 429 — the two do not fight. Six
tests cover the retry, the no-header and too-long cases, the second 429,
the ceiling arithmetic, and both header forms.

## Verified

API **1303/1303** (eleven tests added), ruff clean, mypy at **51** — it
rose to 54 on two unannotated helpers, and annotating them and the
extractor took it one below where it started — with the web, design-system and shared-types figures unchanged
from the entry above (no web file touched here).

# Google Sign-In, second pass: the feature already existed; audited against the new brief, seven gaps closed, first contact with real Google made, the consent-screen step still the founder's

**2026-09-21.** The brief opened with "there is no Google OAuth code
anywhere in this repository", confirmed by search. The search was of some
other tree: Epic 20 (commit `34084a1`, 2026-09-10) built the feature on
both sides — the three settings, PKCE with Redis state and nonce, JWKS
verification through PyJWT, the four routes, the linking policy, the
migration with the renamed credential CHECK, `signInMethods`, the branded
button on both panels, the completion page, the front-door sentences and
the Settings copy — with 21 API tests. What Epic 20 never had, and said
so, was a real Google round trip. So this pass did what the brief actually
needed: audited the existing implementation against every sentence of
the new spec, closed what fell short, and took the live provider as far
toward real Google as a script can go.

## The audit, and what it found

Eight readers, one per requirement group, each returning file:line
verdicts against the brief's literal text (68 requirements); a
second round of two skeptics per verdict was cut short by an API session
limit after 23 of 149 votes, all of which agreed with the readers. Of the
68: 57 met, 9 partial, 2 missing. The gaps, and what was done:

1. **A blank Google setting counted as configured.** `cp .env.example
   .env` leaves `GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=` present and empty; the check was
   `is not None`, so the button sent a browser to Google with an empty
   client id instead of answering the 503 `.env.example` promises. A
   validator now reads a blank as unset; tested. The other provider keys
   keep their `is None` reading (`provider_key`), noted, not changed.
2. **The refusal reasons were deliberately coarse, and the brief asks
   for them told apart.** Suspended, claimed-by-a-different-Google-account
   and no-live-invitation all read `account-unavailable`, on Epic 20's
   argument that the front door should not say which. Reversed, on the
   brief's instruction and a better reading of who is standing there: the
   person has just proven, through Google, that they hold the very email
   address in question, so `account-suspended`, `email-claimed` and
   `invitation-expired` each tell the address's own holder about their own
   seat and nobody else anything. A soft-deleted account stays
   `account-unavailable`. The front door has a sentence for each; the
   contract lists them; the module docstring records the reversal.
3. **The callback could still show a raw 500.** "Always a 302" held for
   every refusal the route knew about, not for Redis or Postgres failing
   underneath it. The route body is wrapped; anything unexpected is logged
   and becomes `reason=unavailable` with a rollback attempted; tested by
   breaking the flow store.
4. **Re-sending an invitation cleared the Google link on one branch of
   two.** The revive branch nulled `google_sub`; the INVITED re-issue
   branch did not. Nothing writes a sub onto an INVITED row today, but the
   rule is unconditional and is now implemented and tested that way.
5. **The licence audit had never decided `cffi`.** PyJWT's `crypto` extra
   pulls `cryptography` (Apache-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause), `cffi` and
   `pycparser` (BSD-3-Clause); `cffi` is MIT-0 — MIT with the attribution
   clause removed, strictly more permissive — and sat on the audit's
   REVIEW list from Epic 20 until now. `MIT-0` is in the allowed set with
   the reasoning beside it, the dependency line in `pyproject.toml` says
   what it pulls in, and the audit now prints four REVIEW lines, all of
   them older than Epic 20.
6. **`verify_id_token` ran on the event loop.** PyJWT fetches the JWKS
   with urllib on a cold cache (a 30s default timeout) and the RSA verify
   is CPU work; `exchange` now runs it in a thread, so a slow first fetch
   stalls one sign-in and not every request in the process.
7. **The live provider had zero tests, and the web side had none for the
   button's presence, the sentences, or the Settings copy.** Added:
   `test_google_live_provider.py` (the authorization URL's every
   parameter; a good token; the legacy issuer form; wrong audience,
   wrong issuer, expired, missing claims; a token signed by a key Google
   never issued; HS256 over the public key and `alg: none`, both built by
   hand because PyJWT's own encoder refuses them; the exchange's form
   fields; a refused exchange, a 200 without a token, a transport
   failure, a bad token from a good exchange); in the integration file, a
   deleted account, a revoked invitation, the re-send rule, the blank
   setting, the infrastructure failure, and ticket expiry driven by a
   one-second TTL rather than inferred from `ex=`; on the web, the
   sentence mapping (extracted to `lib/auth/googleFailure.ts` so a static
   render can test what `Home` reads in an effect), the button on each
   panel under its "or" rule with the form still present, and the Settings
   section for a Google-only account against a password one.

**Judged met as built, with the difference named.** The completion page
asks for the agency name and the person's name, pre-filled from Google;
the brief says "the one thing this flow can't get from Google". Google's
`name` claim can be empty or a handle, and `POST /complete` requires a
name, so the field stays: pre-filled, and a person who agrees with Google
types only the agency. The completion panel's submit and error paths have
static tests only, per the repo's Epic 9.11 rule of no DOM-driving
harness, which the brief's "fetch-driven" tests would have needed.

## First contact with real Google, without anyone's account

`scripts/verify_google_live.py`, step 0, against Google's live
infrastructure through the module's own code — the first time
`LiveGoogleProvider` has touched anything but the suite's fake:

| | result |
|---|---|
| discovery document vs the pinned authorization, token and JWKS endpoints and issuer | all four match |
| `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported` | `["RS256"]`, the verifier's pin |
| the real JWKS through the verifier's own `jwt.PyJWKClient` | 2 signing keys, both RS256 |
| a token signed by a key Google never issued | refused (`PyJWKClientError` → `GoogleExchangeError`) |
| a bogus code at the real token endpoint, through `exchange` | 400 → `GoogleExchangeError` → `exchange-failed` |

Steps 1–4 of the same script run against the deployed API: the 302 to
`accounts.google.com` with the client id, this deployment's redirect URI,
S256, state, nonce, the three scopes and `prompt=select_account`; the
Cancel path consuming the state; the same state refused a second time;
`/pending` refusing a bogus ticket. They print the exact consent-screen
URL the API minted for a person to open.

## What is not done, and why it is not this pass's to do

**The deployed URL is not in this repository** — no `render.yaml`, no
hostname in any config or doc; the brief's Render service and its three
environment variables live in the founder's account. And **the consent
screen needs the founder's own Google account**, the test user on the
OAuth client. Steps 1–4 run the moment the base URL is given, and the
round trip is proven by landing on `/dashboard` signed in after the
person consents. Neither can be substituted by a script, and this entry
does not claim either.

## Verified

Before: API **1303/1303**, web **843/843**, design-system **622/622**,
shared-types **53**, both typechecks clean, ruff clean, mypy at 51.
After: API **1324/1324** (21 tests added across the two Google files),
web **853/853** (10 added), design-system and shared-types unchanged,
both typechecks clean, ruff clean, mypy at 51. The licence audit: four
REVIEW lines (`certifi`, `pathspec` on MPL-2.0; `email-validator` on the
Unlicense; the app itself), none from this feature.

**Pushed, and CI said no — 2026-09-22.** Nine commits had accumulated
since Epic 18.2's last green run without a push, so the gate had not run
on any of them; on `ed33208` it failed one step: `api-mypy-errors: 51
errors, ceiling is 50`. The ceiling was set at 50 by Epic 18 and the count
drifted to 53 through Epics 19–21, which every cost-pass entry recorded
and none was allowed to fix as its own scope. Fixed here by typing three
bare generics in `engines.py` (`dict[str, Any]` twice, `list[Any]` once):
**48**, under the ceiling by two, and the ceiling itself is untouched — it
is a ceiling. The same local run then showed one failure the hour-earlier
run had not: the Perplexity pacer test measured a 27ms gap under a 50ms
interval. Not the pacer: the test timed request ARRIVALS at a fake
transport, and a loaded machine scheduled one admitted task late. It now
reads the pacer's own admission instants (`_next_allowed - interval`),
exact by construction; five runs alone and one full suite, all green. The
consent-screen probe against the real deployment, run the same day, is
the next entry's subject.

# Google Sign-In against the real deployment: every step a script can take passes; the consent screen is the founder's next click

**2026-09-22.** The founder gave the deployed API's base URL,
`https://ai-visibility-platform-5gk4.onrender.com/api/v1`, and
`scripts/verify_google_live.py` ran against it. No credential was sent
and nothing was created.

| step | against | result |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Google's discovery document, JWKS, and token endpoint, through the module's own code | endpoints and issuer match, JWKS yields 2 RS256 keys, a forged token is refused, a bogus code is `exchange-failed` |
| 1 | `GET /auth/google/start` on the deployment | **302** to `accounts.google.com`, carrying the real client id (`192749258566-…apps.googleusercontent.com`), `redirect_uri` = this deployment's own callback, `state`, `nonce`, `code_challenge`, `S256`, `openid email profile`, `prompt=select_account` — so all three `GOOGLE_OAUTH_*` variables are set on the host and read |
| 2 | the callback with Google's Cancel (`error=access_denied`) and that state | 302 to `https://ai-visibility-platform-1.onrender.com/?google=error&reason=denied` — the state store (Redis on the host) consumed it |
| 3 | the same state again | 302 with `reason=invalid-state` — single use holds on the real store |
| 4 | `GET /auth/google/pending?ticket=bogus` | `400 invalid-google-ticket` |

The failure redirects land on the web app's host,
`ai-visibility-platform-1.onrender.com`, which is `PUBLIC_WEB_BASE_URL`
on the API service; that front door and its `/sign-up/google` page both
answer 200, and the API's `/health` does. **Not yet done, and only the
founder can do it:** open the consent URL the script prints (or press
the button on the deployed front door, which mints a fresh one — the
printed one is single-use and ten minutes), choose the test-user account,
consent, and land on `/dashboard` signed in. That landing is the round
trip; nothing here claims it.

# The report visualisations, extended: a share strip for the one gap that was real, the verdict strip generalised for the two thin pages, and what the brief assumed that the tree did not bear out

**2026-09-22.** The brief came with a market catalogue of chart shapes, a
real scan to build against, and an instruction to verify the tree before
trusting any of it. Verified first; three of its premises did not hold,
one gap was genuine, and the two thin pages needed a different shape from
the one it expected. No chart library was imported; everything below is
the house's own SVG and CSS, under the same rules as every shape before it.

## What was found to exist, against what the brief assumed

- **`/clients/{id}/rankings` and `/sources` are real pages**, not
  unbuilt ones: both routes render `ClientRankingsView` and
  `ClientSourcesView`, exported from `ClientDetailView.tsx` since Epic
  9.20 — a naming mismatch, not missing work. Rankings is share of voice
  over time as a `TrendChart`; Sources is citations per domain over time.
- **Share of voice at ONE moment was the genuine gap.** It existed only as
  lines over time (Rankings) and as numbers in each rival's card
  (Competitors). Nothing drew the field divided at a single scan, and a
  client scanned once — the state every new client is in — got an empty
  state on Rankings, because a trend needs two points. `LuminanceLedger`
  was checked and is not it: it is one brand's dimensions, not a field's
  shares.
- **The Prompts page has no time series to draw.** It is the operator's
  prompt-run screen (Epic 9.24), and its own docstring forbids a run from
  ever appearing in a trend, because a question an operator typed is not
  a measurement. `TrendChart` would have been the wrong claim, not the
  wrong chart.
- **The Crawler page has no activity to draw.** It reads a robots.txt
  policy — what the site *asks* each crawler — and `ClientCrawlerView.test`
  forbids the words "activity", "visits", "traffic", "hits", because no
  crawl log is ingested anywhere. A bar chart of crawl activity by day,
  the PromptWatch shape the brief pointed at, cannot exist here honestly.
- **A competitor-by-engine sentiment heatmap cannot exist either.**
  Sentiment is classified toward the subject only (scoring-spec rule 4);
  rivals have no tone. The subject-by-engine row already exists in the
  report's cross-engine reading. Not built, and this says why.
- **`VerdictBar` already was a proportional strip.** Pass / warn / fail as
  one bar with semantic tones and a legend that is its own data table —
  the shape the two thin pages needed, with different categories.

## Built

**`ShareBar`** (`packages/design-system/src/components/chart/ShareBar.tsx`,
`shareLayout.ts`): share of voice at one scan as one divided strip whose
segment widths *are* the shares. A strip and not the donut both rivals
lead with, for two reasons recorded in `design-system.md` §5f: every shape
in this system encodes by length, and a donut wants a wedge for every
brand — which is exactly how a zero-share rival becomes a confident slice.
Here a **measured zero is never drawn**; it is a line in the legend and
the hidden table, *"0%, named in none of the answers"*, and an
**unmeasured** share says *"not measured"*. The layout keeps the two
apart. Brands the engines named that nobody tracks are an **outlined
remainder** so the strip still sums to the whole — but only when at least
one share was measured; nothing measured, nothing claimed. Subject beacon,
rivals from `seriesStyle` with a fill pattern each, the visibility ramp
never touched, `ChartFrame`'s accessibility contract, bounded at its drawn
width.

**Tested against the real scan, not invented numbers.** The MSM AV field
of 22 Sept 2026 (subject 0.0; Sweetwater 38.5, Shure 26.1, AVI-SPL 18.5,
Diversified 16.9, Avalliance 0.0) is the layout's fixture
(`shareLayout.fixtures.ts`, real data kept out of the styleguide's
fictional fixtures on purpose): four segments, largest first; Avalliance
no segment and a stated absence; the subject listed first as absent and
marked as this client; widths equal to the shares; no remainder because
the four sum to the whole. Twelve more cases cover null, the remainder,
the rounding floor, overshoot scaled back, subject-first ordering, and the
all-zero field.

**`VerdictBar` gained `segments`**: any ordered list of named integers with
a tone — the semantic three, `neutral`, `beacon` for the one segment that
is the client, and `none` for "nothing decided", unpainted track with an
inset line so it counts as a segment and does not read as a gap. The
`counts` path is byte-for-byte unchanged, asserted.

**Wired:**

- **Rankings** shows the strip above the trend — the split, then the
  direction — and a client scanned once now gets the split *and* the
  "one scan is not a trend yet" note instead of the note alone.
  `shareSplit()` in `lib/client/trends.ts` reads the latest scan with a
  reading, subject first, passing a measured `0.00` as zero and an absent
  reading as null. The caption states the subject's share in words, and
  for MSM AV says it was named in none of the answers.
- **Crawler**: one strip per purpose group, by verdict, with the group's
  existing vocabulary — blocked (danger), not readable (warn), allowed
  (neutral, deliberately not success), not mentioned (`none`). Only the
  verdicts a group holds are listed: the existing guard caught the first
  draft printing "Not mentioned 0" under an unreadable robots.txt, which
  is the permissive claim that test exists to refuse.
- **Prompts**: one strip per run in its header — named you (beacon), did
  not name you (neutral, the finding), did not answer (warn, the failure),
  kept apart as the cards below already keep them. The PromptWatch-style
  inline indicator the brief suggested, rather than a chart the data
  could not support.

## Not built, and why

The Competitors page did not get a second copy of the split; Rankings is
share of voice's home and one shape in one place is the rule. The report
document was not touched: its beats are the design review's, and adding a
shape to a printed document is a pass of its own. Positional scoring, the
citation authority taxonomy and query fan-out are scoring and product
changes the brief itself put out of scope; the Prompts strip leaves the
position where the cards already print it.

## Verified

Before: API **1324/1324**, web **843/843**, design-system **622/622**,
shared-types **53**, both typechecks clean, ruff clean, mypy at 48.
After: design-system **647/647** (25 added: 13 layout, 12 render), web
**865/865** (12 added across Rankings, Crawler, Prompts and the trend
helpers), API, shared-types, typechecks, ruff and mypy unchanged.
`design-system.md` §5f records the shape and the `VerdictBar` extension;
the styleguide carries a section for the strip on its invented company.

## The one defect only a screenshot could catch

The subject's legend line read **"MSM AV· this client"** — the space before
the middle dot was gone. The label is `inline-flex`; the "· this client"
span is therefore a flex item; and a flex item's leading collapsible space
is dropped at layout. The text node carries the space, `renderToStaticMarkup`
prints it, and every static test passes — the defect exists only once the
browser lays the line out, which is precisely the class of thing "actually
look at it" exists to find. Fix: `white-space: pre-wrap` on
`.avp-share__you`, one line of CSS with the reason beside it; no markup and
no test changed, and the corrected render is the screenshot that was kept.

## Not built, and why — the Dashboard

- **An agency-wide visibility trend cannot be built today.** `DashboardOut`
  is `recent_scans` — a bounded list, one composite per scan, in no
  particular window — plus counts. Nothing in the API aggregates composite
  scores across the client book over time: no endpoint, no schema field, no
  service that reads `client_history` for more than one client. A trend
  drawn from `recent_scans` would be a line through whichever scans happen
  to be on the first page, of whichever clients happen to have run, and
  would read as the agency's trajectory when it is a page of a table. It
  needs new backend work — an aggregation endpoint or a schema addition —
  and that is a separate decision, not scoped or designed here.
- **An agency-wide Share of Voice is not a coherent figure as things
  stand.** Share of Voice is a division of one field: the subject against
  ITS competitors, detected independently per client. Two clients have two
  different fields with no shared denominator — MSM AV's Sweetwater and
  Shure are not in a dental practice's field — so there is no single field
  to divide at the agency level, and a strip that showed one would imply a
  distribution that does not exist. This is the same call the report
  visualisations pass made against a competitor-by-engine sentiment
  heatmap, when sentiment is classified toward the subject only: the number
  the chart would need is not one the system measures. Said here rather
  than approximated.

# Citation Strength gets an authority input, part one: the lookup — a curated tier, a platform-frequency tier, and the measurement that decided against a table

**2026-09-27.** The first of three checkpoints on one brief. Citation
Strength has been excluded from the composite since v2.1 because §6 asks
for "number AND authority of domains citing the brand" and nothing in the
system produced authority. This checkpoint adds the input and nothing
else: the scoring change and the report copy follow in their own commits.

## What was verified before writing

- **`HEAD` was `7f83161`, equal to `origin/main`, tree clean** apart from
  the same four untracked skill-repository directories as the last pass.
- **`citation_strength()` still divides the subject's own domain by every
  distinct third-party domain in the scan**, and `compute_score` still
  excludes it under `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` with the `else` branch marked
  "unreachable today". The 33-scores / 3.70-maximum figure in the constant's
  comment describes the day of v2.1 and still holds for what it describes:
  `avp_dev` now carries 41 score rows — 15 `v1.1`, 18 `v2`, 8 `v2.1` — and
  the maximum `citation_strength` on the 32 rows that have one is 3.70. The
  eight `v2.1` rows carry null, as the exclusion says they should.
- **`competitors.py`'s docstring still names Finding 2 as open**, and the
  build log's Epic 2.8 entry still records the post-tuning confidence run as
  0.95, 0.97, 0.97, 0.96, 0.96 — clustered, uncalibrated, untouched since.

## Built — `services/domain_authority.py`

**Tier A, curated and structural.** Matched by suffix for `.gov`, `.edu`,
`.mil` and their country forms (`gov`/`edu`/`ac`/`mil`/`gouv`/`gob`/
`govt`/`gc`/`go` under a two-letter code, with a name in front — so
`go.com` and a bare `gov.uk` are not caught); by name for Wikipedia,
Wikidata, AP (`apnews.com`, `ap.org`), Reuters, BBB, Trustpilot, G2 and
Capterra, each as itself or a subdomain; and Capterra additionally on its
first label with a public-suffix-shaped tail, because its country editions
(`capterra.co.uk`, `capterra.ca`, `capterra.com.de`) were all cited in real
scans. `capterra.example.com` does not match. Nothing is on the list for
being judged reliable; each entry is there for a structural reason the
module docstring states. General news, forums and industry-specific
authorities are excluded on purpose — the last group is Tier B's job.

**Tier B, platform frequency.** A domain qualifies when cited across at
least **3** distinct `Client.industry` values and at least **5** distinct
clients. One `GROUP BY ... HAVING` over `engine_result_citations` joined
through `engine_results` and `scans` to `clients`, industry non-null,
client not soft-deleted. **Both thresholds are first guesses**, said so in
the code comment: three because two industries can be one market under two
labels, five so that no single source-heavy scan can qualify a domain
alone. Neither was derived from data because there is not yet enough data
to derive from.

**What Tier A finds in the stored rows today:** g2.com (145 citations),
capterra.com (112), trustpilot.com (17), wikipedia.org (9), bbb.org (4),
three Capterra country editions and two `.edu` domains at one each. No
`.gov`, no wire service — the stored scans are software-buyer questions.

## Live aggregate, not a materialised table — measured

`avp_dev` on the day: **5,787 citation rows, 1,552 distinct domains, 395
engine results, 27 clients, 12 industry labels.** `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,
BUFFERS)` on the exact Tier B statement: **planning 7.3 ms, execution 15.2
ms**, 3,589 shared buffers hit, the citations side an index-only scan on
`ix_citations_result_domain`. Scoring runs once per scan chain and once per
explicit re-score; a 15 ms aggregate on that path does not justify a
refresh schedule, a staleness window and a migration. The docstring names
the size at which to revisit and what to try first.

## What the thresholds admit today — recorded, not softened

Run against the real rows, the 3-industry / 5-client rule admits **70
domains**. The top of the list is what the tier is for — g2.com across 10
industries and 21 clients, capterra.com 10 and 17, softwareadvice.com 8
and 12, trustradius.com 8 and 11, getapp.com 7 and 12 — but a good part of
it is vendors in one market: eesel.ai (7 industries, 14 clients),
get-alfred.ai (7, 13), featurebase.app (7, 12), getmacha.com (6, 12),
hiverhq.com (6, 12), zendesk.com (4, 8). They clear "seven industries"
because the labels split help-desk software into "customer service
software" (6 clients), "customer support software" (2), "help desk
software" (1), "customer support helpdesk software" (1) and "team
collaboration and email software" (1). That is the coarse-proxy limitation
in the flesh, and it is exactly what an uncalibrated classification cannot
screen out. The thresholds stay where the brief put them; this paragraph is
the evidence for the revisit.

# Citation Strength gets an authority input, part two: the scoring change — v3, the tier values argued, the no-rival case decided, and what the new number does to every stored scan

**2026-09-27.** Second checkpoint. `citation_strength()` now reads the
lookup part one built; `compute_score` includes the dimension whenever the
scan has a classifiable citation and a rival to compare against;
`FORMULA_VERSION` is `v3`. The report copy that explains all this to a
reader is part three.

## What changed in `services/scoring.py`

- **`citation_strength(results, competitors, *, authority)`.** A brand's
  citing domains are the distinct third-party sources cited in answered
  results that NAME the brand — `mentioned` for the subject, the rival's
  name in `brands` for a competitor — less the brand's own domain, which is
  not a third party to itself. Each carries its tier's value; the subject's
  sum is normalised against the largest sum in the scan. That is the rule
  scoring-spec.md stated for this dimension from the start and the thing
  the v1–v2 stand-in never did: its "subject's citations" were the
  `cites_subject` rows, which are the subject's own domain, 0 or 1, over
  every domain cited — hence 1/N and the 3.70 ceiling. The docstring keeps
  that account and says what replaced it.
- **`AUTHORITY_VALUES` — curated 100, platform 50, unclassified 0.** Only
  the ratios matter under normalisation. Curated is the ceiling by
  construction: nothing in this system is stronger evidence than a `.gov`,
  a university, a reference work, a wire service or a cross-industry review
  platform. Unclassified is zero because no tier is no evidence, the same
  as its absence before v3. Platform sits at the midpoint for the reason
  neutral sentiment does: it states the ordering — worth more than nothing,
  less than a structural fact — and claims nothing about where between the
  two it falls, because the tier is measured through an uncalibrated
  industry label and any other number would imply a measurement nobody has
  made. The 100/60/25 in the brief were placeholders; 25 for unclassified
  would have contradicted the brief's own tier definition ("contributes
  zero authority weight") and made a scan of forty blogs score, which is
  not what "number AND authority" means when only the number is known.
- **Two exclusions.** `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` fires only when no cited domain
  in the scan has a tier — no input, exactly v2.1's situation, exactly
  v2.1's behaviour, and the test that says so asserts the flag list is
  `["NO_AUTHORITY_DATA"]` and nothing else. **`NO_COMPETITOR_SET` fires
  when tiered domains were cited but no competitor set exists**, a case
  the brief did not name and the code had to decide. The figure is the
  subject against the best in the scan; with no rival the best in the scan
  is the subject, and any classifiable citation would read 100 — a full
  mark for a detection failure, which is the v1 Share of Voice defect and
  gets the v1.1 answer, under the same code Share of Voice already uses.
  `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` takes precedence when both hold, so the no-input
  case is untouched. `NO_CITATIONS_IN_SCAN` is still a flag either way.
- **Rivals' column.** `compare_competitors` gives each rival its own sum
  against the same denominator, so the best-cited brand in the table reads
  100 and the rest read their distance from it. Still `None` whenever the
  subject's is excluded — a column means one thing.
- **The tiers are in the digest.** Tier B is a frequency over the whole
  platform's stored scans and moves as they accumulate; the same results
  re-scored a month on can carry a different number under the same
  formula. `compute_inputs_digest` now takes `domain_tiers` — the tier of
  every cited domain in the scan that has one, and only those, so a
  domain outside the scan entering Tier B does not move the digest. The
  third time that function has been widened for rule 1, after
  `technical_foundation` and `intent`.
- **`v3`, not `v2.3`.** v2 was a major bump because the population change
  moved every composite. A dimension re-entering the weighting moves every
  composite with a classifiable citation, by up to its full 20 points. Same
  precedent, same size of bump. Rows carrying `v2.1` keep their numbers.
- **`scoring_runner.score_scan` loads the lookup** with
  `load_domain_authority(session)` on every scoring and passes it through;
  `compute_score`'s default is the curated tier alone and its docstring
  says that default is for unit tests and wrong for production.

## What the new number does to the stored scans — measured, not persisted

`score_scan(persist=False)` over the 26 scans in `avp_dev` that carry a
score, against the live lookup (70 platform domains). **Citation Strength
is measured on 23**; one is `NO_ANSWERED_RESULTS`, one `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA`
(a helpwise.io scan whose 11 answers cited nothing tiered), one
`NO_COMPETITOR_SET` (ghost.org, 96.67 composite with no rival set). The
composite moves **+3.04 to +20.00** against the latest stored row on every
measured scan, because a dimension came back at a value of 25 to 100.

**And the value is 100 on 14 of the 23.** helpscout.com, basecamp.com,
linear.app, three plausible.io runs, two notion.so runs, front.com,
missiveapp.com, intercom.com, hiverhq.com — all 100. The rest: zammad.com
89.47, helpwise.io 90.63 / 82.61 / 33.33, pirsch.io 55.00, reamaze.com
61.90, groovehq.com 32.00, psmdigitalagency 25.00 to 62.50. Median 100.

## The mechanism, and a finding for a decision rather than a fix

The subject is credited every tiered domain cited in any answer that
names it. Citation Strength keeps EVERY answered result — scoring-spec.md
says so, "decided, not pending", and gives sentiment's reasoning: how an
answer portrays a brand is a real signal whether the buyer named it or
not. But co-occurrence attribution makes this dimension different from
sentiment in exactly the way v2 found Mention Rate was: **a question that
names the brand guarantees the brand co-occurs with whatever that answer
cites.** 55% of a prompt set names the subject by construction, so the
subject accumulates the union of the scan's tiered sources almost
regardless of standing, while each rival accumulates only what was cited
where an engine chose to name it.

Measured the other way, on awareness prompts only, per scan
(all-answered → awareness-only, with the awareness-only Mention Rate):

| client | all answered | awareness only | awareness MR |
|---|---|---|---|
| helpwise.io | 90.63 | **0** | 0 |
| helpwise.io | 82.61 | **0** | 0 |
| helpwise.io | 33.33 | **0** | 0 |
| groovehq.com | 32.00 | **0** | 0 |
| psmdigitalagency.com | 33.33 | **0** | 0 |
| psmdigitalagency.com.au (×3) | 25.00 / 62.50 / 50.00 | excluded / 0 / 0 | 0 |
| zammad.com | 89.47 | 18.18 | 63.64 |
| reamaze.com | 61.90 | 7.14 | 25.64 |
| pirsch.io | 55.00 | 40.00 | 30.56 |
| hiverhq.com | 100 | 93.10 | 68.42 |
| missiveapp.com | 100 | 90.91 | 91.67 |
| the nine at 100 with MR ≥ 94 | 100 | 100 | 94–100 |

helpwise.io reads 90.63 on a scan where no unprompted question named it at
all: every point of that 90 came from answers to questions that supplied
the name. That is the v2 tautology, arriving through a different door.

**Not changed here.** The population is a scoring POLICY the spec closed
with a stated reason and said would need "a reason of its own" to reopen.
This is that reason, and it is recorded for the founder to decide, not
applied on the way past: the brief specified the formula, said nothing
about the population, and a second unrequested policy change inside a
formula bump would be exactly the silent restating of history rule 5
forbids. What the table shows is that the choice is material — on the
five clients who are invisible unprompted, it is the difference between a
Citation Strength of 25–90 and one of 0 — and that the dimension as
shipped will read as strong on any brand a prompt set names by
construction. The copy in part three says the figure is measured on every
answered result, so a reader is at least not told otherwise.

## Docs

scoring-spec.md: table row 3, a new "measured from a two-tier authority
input (v3)" section above the v2.1 section (which now reads in the past
tense), two edge-case rows, and a `v3` changelog entry in the format the
v2/v2.1 rows use. api-contracts.md: the `ScoreDetailOut` example is a v3
score with five weights and a rival at `100.00`, the reasons table has the
new meaning of `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` and the Citation Strength
`NO_COMPETITOR_SET` row, and the paragraph on the rivals' column says what
it carries now.

## Verified

API **1401/1401** (was 1324; +65 lookup tests in part one, +12 here),
exit code read from a file. `test_scoring.py`'s citation classes rewritten
for v3: a curated domain scoring with no platform data, a platform domain
at its tier, an unclassified domain at zero, nothing classifiable flagging
`NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` and nothing else, no citations flagged distinctly,
normalisation against the best rival (150 against 250 → 60), the best
brand reading 100 whoever it is, distinct domains not raw counts, own
domains earning nothing for subject or rival, co-occurrence credited to
both, unanswered and unnaming results not counted, five dimensions
weighted and re-summing exactly when scored, rivals against the same best,
`NO_COMPETITOR_SET` for the no-rival case, precedence of `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA`,
the tiers moving the digest and an out-of-scan domain not moving it. One
end-to-end test in `test_domain_authority.py` takes seeded rows through
`load_domain_authority` into `compute_score` and watches the exclusion
turn into a measurement. `test_client_history.py`'s "rivals carry null"
assertion now says the opposite, with the reason. ruff clean; mypy 48
before and after (the two errors mypy reports in scoring.py are on lines
this change did not touch, and the count did not move).

**2026-09-27.** Third checkpoint. The scoring now produces a number; this
is what the report says about it, in the PDF and on screen, held to the
same bytes by a fixture the way the gap arithmetic already is.

## Built

# Citation Strength gets an authority input — the whole pass in one place: the thresholds chosen, the tier values chosen, and the limitation stated in full

**2026-09-27.** Three checkpoints (`6a8ff38` the lookup, `7689528` the
scoring, `3f234b9` the copy) and this summary, pushed together. A reader
who opens only this entry should have every number and every caveat.

## The thresholds — Tier B

A domain is platform-tier when stored scans have cited it across **at
least 3 distinct `Client.industry` values and at least 5 distinct
clients**, industry non-null, client not soft-deleted, computed live (15 ms
on 5,787 rows, measured; no table). **Both are first guesses.** Three
industries because two can be one market under two labels; five clients so
no single source-heavy scan qualifies a domain alone. Neither was derived
from data: 27 clients over 12 labels is not a base to derive from. On
those 27 clients the rule admits **70 domains**, and the list is honest
about what that means — g2.com (10 industries, 21 clients) and
softwareadvice.com (8, 12) at the top, and eesel.ai (7, 14), featurebase.app
(7, 12), hiverhq.com (6, 12), zendesk.com (4, 8) further down: help-desk
vendors that count as "seven industries" because the labels split one
market five ways. Revisit with real volume; the docstring says where to
look first.

## The tier values — `AUTHORITY_VALUES`

**Curated 100, platform 50, unclassified 0.** Only the ratios matter, since
the subject's sum is normalised against the best in the scan. Curated is
the ceiling by construction. Unclassified is zero because no tier is no
evidence, the same as its absence before v3. Platform is the midpoint for
the reason neutral sentiment is: it states the ordering and claims no
precision the proxy does not have. The brief's 100 / 60 / 25 were
placeholders; 25 for unclassified would have contradicted the brief's own
tier definition and scored a scan of forty blogs.

## What the score is

A brand's citing domains are the third-party sources cited in answered
results that name it, less its own domain; each carries its tier value;
`citation_strength = 100 × subject's sum / best sum in the scan`, rivals
against the same denominator. `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` when no cited domain has
a tier (unchanged behaviour from v2.1); `NO_COMPETITOR_SET` when tiered
domains were cited but there is no rival to normalise against. Formula
`v3`; `v2.1` rows are not re-scored; the tiers are in the inputs digest.

## The limitation, in full and unsoftened

Tier B counts industries through `Client.industry`, and that label's
classification confidence score was found uncalibrated in Epic 2.6 —
**five real sites scored 0.97, 0.97, 0.97, 0.97, 0.96**, effectively one
value against a prompt that asked for the full range — re-measured after
Epic 2.8's tuning at 0.95, 0.97, 0.97, 0.96, 0.96, and **never fixed
since**. The `CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD = 0.70` ambiguity path has never fired
on a real site. So there is **no reliable way to screen a mis-classified
client's industry out of the Tier B count**: a client the classifier put
in the wrong industry contributes a wrong industry to every domain its
scans cite, with a confidence score that says 0.97 either way. The label
itself is more workable than the number — Finding 1's over-generalisation
("b2b saas", "technology company") was addressed with prompt tuning — but
the fragmentation the 70-domain list shows is the other face of the same
coin: labels fine enough to be specific are fine enough to split one
market into several "industries". Industry-spread is therefore a **coarse
proxy that cannot currently filter out a bad classification**, and it is
weighted at half the curated tier for that reason. The report says this
to the reader in `DIMENSION_NOTE` and in the `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` detail,
in the PDF and on screen, and both suites assert the words "uncalibrated",
"coarse proxy" and "mis-classified" are present.

## The second finding, for a decision

Measured on the 23 stored scans the dimension now scores: **100 on 14**,
composites up **+3.04 to +20.00**. The mechanism is co-occurrence plus
the every-answered-result population: a question that names the brand
guarantees the brand co-occurs with whatever the answer cites, and 55% of
a prompt set names it by construction. helpwise.io reads 90.63 on a scan
where no unprompted question named it; on awareness prompts alone five
clients drop to 0. Part two has the table. Not changed — the population
is a policy the spec closed with a reason and this is the reason of its
own it asked for — and recorded here so the choice is made deliberately.

## Verified, final

API **1408/1408**, web **882/882**, design-system **648/648**,
shared-types **53**, both typechecks clean, ruff clean, mypy **48** under
the ceiling of 50, every exit code read from a file. CI: see the push.

# Citation Strength on the awareness population — section 1 of three: the closed policy reopened for a reason of its own, rivals on the same population, and three exclusions in a stated order

**2026-09-27.** First of three checkpoints on one brief; sections 1 and 2
ship under one formula bump, `v4`, and section 3 changes no score.

## What was verified before writing

- **`HEAD` was `006746a`, equal to `origin/main`.** The tree carried one
  unintended change: `packages/design-system/dist-styleguide/` (a tracked
  build output) had been regenerated by the previous pass's `pnpm build`
  with new asset hashes. Restored with `git checkout` before anything else;
  the four untracked skill-repository directories remain untracked.
- **`authority_sums()` still summed over every answered result**, for the
  subject (`mentioned`) and each rival (name in `brands`); `citation_strength()`
  and `compare_competitors()` both handed it `answered`, not `aware`.
  `awareness_only()` is unchanged since v2. `load_platform_domains()` still
  filters on industry non-null and client not deleted, nothing else.
- **The part-two table holds against the data**: the `all answered` versus
  `awareness only` script from that entry re-run today gives the same rows —
  helpwise.io 90.63 → 0 with awareness Mention Rate 0, groovehq.com 32.00 →
  0, zammad.com 89.47 → 18.18, reamaze.com 61.90 → 7.14.
- **The sentence to replace exists in six places**: `strings.ts`,
  `report_narrative.py`, `report-copy.json`, `copyContract.test.ts`,
  `test_report_copy.py`, `ReportView.test.tsx`. Section 2 moves them all.

## The change

`citation_strength` and `compare_competitors` hand `authority_sums` the
awareness results — the subject's sum and every rival's, so the column keeps
one denominator and one population. `NO_CITATIONS_IN_SCAN` is still decided
over the whole scan, because it is a fact about the scan.

**The spec's closed question, reopened in the spec.** scoring-spec.md's
population section said "Sentiment and Citation Strength keep every answered
result. Decided, not pending," and that reopening needed "a reason of its
own". The paragraph now splits: sentiment keeps its paragraph and its
reasoning unchanged; Citation Strength gets its own, stating the reason —
attribution is by co-occurrence and a brand-named question manufactures it —
and why sentiment's argument does not carry over: portrayal is a property of
the answer, co-occurrence with a source is a property of the question that
produced the answer.

**Edge cases, decided.** Three exclusions in a fixed order, and the order has
a reason recorded in the `compute_score` comment: `NO_AWARENESS_POPULATION`
first (a fact about the population — with nothing in it the other two
questions have no subject), `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` second (a fact about the
input — the awareness answers cite nothing tiered; brand-named answers citing
tiered sources do not rescue it, because that is the co-occurrence the change
exists to stop counting), `NO_COMPETITOR_SET` third (a fact about the
comparison, which only arises once there is something to compare).

**`FORMULA_VERSION = "v4"`.** The constant's comment and the changelog row
cover both sections; the row is written now and names section 2's exclusion,
which the next checkpoint lands. Major, not minor: v2's population change
was major and v2.1's exclusion minor, and this is a population change first.

## Verified

`test_scoring.py` +7 in a `TestCitationStrengthPopulation` class: a
helpwise-shaped fixture (awareness Mention Rate 0, every brand-named answer
citing curated sources) reads `NO_AUTHORITY_DATA` and nothing else; with one
awareness answer citing g2.com for a rival it scores exactly 0 in the
composite; rivals' figures equal `compare_competitors` run on
`awareness_only` alone; sentiment over one awareness and two brand-named
answers is the mean of all three (66.67); no awareness prompts excludes all
three discovery dimensions under one code; the precedence holds on a fixture
where all three conditions apply, then two, then one; and
`NO_CITATIONS_IN_SCAN` travels beside `NO_AWARENESS_POPULATION`. The full
API bar and the commit follow from the log's exit code.

# Market participants out of Tier B — section 2 of three: the exclusion, its cost re-measured, the admitted list before and after, and what v4 does to every stored scan

**2026-09-27.** Second checkpoint. Section 1 and this one ship under `v4`.

## The change

`load_platform_domains()` refuses, before grouping, any domain that is a
non-deleted `Client.domain` or a non-null `Competitor.domain` anywhere on
the platform — one `UNION` subquery, `NOT IN`. The NULL competitor domains
are filtered out of the subquery explicitly, because `NOT IN` against a set
containing NULL matches nothing, which would have emptied Tier B silently.
Tier A is untouched by construction: `DomainAuthority.tier_of` checks the
curated rule first and never downgrades it, and a test seeds g2.com as a
detected competitor to prove it stays curated. Thresholds unchanged at
3 / 5.

## Cost, re-measured rather than assumed

Three warm `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs with the exclusion: **planning 1.1–1.9 ms,
execution 4.6–6.1 ms.** Two warm runs without it, same session: 5.4 and 5.5
ms. So the two anti-joins cost nothing visible — and the 15 ms recorded in
part one was a cold first run, not the steady state. The docstring now says
both.

## The admitted list, before and after

**70 → 57.** Of the 13 removed, one was a client's own domain
(hiverhq.com) and twelve were detected competitors' domains. Top twenty
before, with what the exclusion did to each:

| g2.com | 10 | 21 | stays (curated anyway) |
| capterra.com | 10 | 17 | stays (curated anyway) |
| checkthat.ai | 9 | 14 | stays |
| softwareadvice.com | 8 | 12 | stays |
| trustradius.com | 8 | 11 | stays |
| eesel.ai | 7 | 14 | **out — competitor** |
| get-alfred.ai | 7 | 13 | stays |
| featurebase.app | 7 | 12 | stays |
| getapp.com | 7 | 12 | stays |
| softwarefinder.com | 7 | 10 | stays |
| cbinsights.com | 7 | 7 | stays |
| getmacha.com | 6 | 12 | stays |
| hiverhq.com | 6 | 12 | **out — client** |
| chatarmin.com | 6 | 9 | stays |
| vendr.com | 6 | 9 | stays |
| github.com | 6 | 8 | stays |

Top twenty after: the eighteen "stays" rows above in the same order, then

(4, 8), helpscout.com and the other detected help-desk rivals went out.

**What the exclusion did not do, said plainly for whoever revisits the

chatarmin.com are vendors — AI support tools that engines list as options —
and they stay, because nobody has scanned them and detection has not named
them. The exclusion is structural, which is its virtue and its limit: it
knows only the market participants the platform has recorded. The list is

**2026-09-27.** Third checkpoint. No score changes here; `v4` is unchanged.

## What was found before writing

  **The subject is stable** — a range of 0.13 and 0.04 of a position, at

  move by up to 0.61 (Airtable), 0.58 (PostHog), 0.45 (Slite), and a rival
  named three times appeared at 5.00 in one run and not at all in the next

  twenty-five answers moved by up to six-tenths of a position" — and the
  reason the figure stays out of the composite in this pass. Stable for the

  the founder and the rival column is the one that moves.

## Built

**`scoring.average_position(results, *, brand=None)`** — mean 1-based
ordinal with the count it is averaged over, Decimal, 2dp. Subject from
`ResultFacts.position` over answered results where `mentioned`; a rival from
the new `ResultFacts.brand_positions` for its name. `(None, 0)` when never
named — never 0, never a large number. `compute_score` calls it on
`awareness_only(answered)` for the subject and `compare_competitors` does
the same per rival; both carry the pair on `ScoreResult` /
`CompetitorComparison`. **Deliberately outside** `compute_inputs_digest`,
`Dimension`, `WEIGHTS` and the Score row, and a test proves a changed
position moves neither the composite, nor a sub-score, nor the digest.

**Derived on read, not stored.** The comparison already is, and for the
same reason: a pure function of rows the database holds, whose second copy
could only fall out of step. So the fields are on `ScoreDetailOut` and
`CompetitorScoreOut` (and their report and history mirrors), set by the
route and the report from `computed`, and not on `ScoreOut`'s list — no
migration, and nothing on the row that could be mistaken for a sub-score.

**Report, both sides.** The rivals table gains an "Average position"
column — `2.4 across 9 answers`, or `Not named` — from `positionCell` /
`position_cell`, one formatter per side producing the same string; the PDF
table now leads with the subject's own row, as the screen's does, so the
column has the comparison it exists for. One line under the table on both
sides says the figure is shown for comparison and does not enter the score,
with the measured reason. `POSITION_COPY` is the sixth table in
`report-copy.json`, regenerated from the TypeScript side.

**Contract.** `scripts/export_openapi.py` then `pnpm generate`: 69 lines in
`openapi.json`, 31 in `api.gen.ts`, both regenerated a second time after
staging to confirm nothing further moves. `api-contracts.md`'s
`ScoreDetailOut` example is a `v4` score carrying the fields, and a
paragraph states what they are, what null means, and why they are not
scored.

# The plan gates something: one free scan, then subscribe — section 2 of two

**2026-09-28.** Until this pass the pricing card said "Nothing in the
product is behind this plan today" and meant it. Stripe was wired to a $160
Price that unlocked nothing. Each scan costs the platform about $1.70 in
engine calls and 6 of the 250 SerpApi searches the Free tier allows a month
— about 41 scans platform-wide before detection stops for everyone. The
decision was made in the brief and is not reopened here: **free is one
completed scan per organisation for life; the plan is forty a calendar
month, UTC; reading is never gated.**

## Built — API

- **`services/scan_allowance.py`.** `FREE_SCAN_ALLOWANCE = 1`,
  `PAID_SCANS_PER_MONTH = 40`, with the arithmetic beside the constant:
  40 × $1.70 ≈ $68 of engine cost against $160, about 57% gross margin
  before SerpApi; and 40 × 6 = 240 searches if every scan were a new client,
  inside the 250. Paid means `services/billing.is_active` — `active` or
  `trialing`; `canceled`, `past_due`, `unpaid`, `paused` are free.
- **What holds a slot.** Every scan not `failed` or `cancelled` — queued and
  running included. The brief's "completed scans only" was taken to mean
  "failures never burn the allowance", which this honours; but a scan in
  flight must count while it is in flight or two requests at the cap both
  see room. The slot is taken when the scan starts and handed back if it
  fails. Said in the module docstring and in api-contracts.md.
- **Enforced in `POST /clients/{id}/scans`, server-side.** `SELECT … FOR
  UPDATE` on the agency row, then the count, then `get_or_create_scan`, then
  the commit that both persists the scan and releases the lock. A second
  concurrent request blocks on the lock, counts the first's committed scan,
  and gets its 402. A plain count-then-insert in one transaction would not
  have closed this at READ COMMITTED; Epic 9.6 found the same shape for the
  per-client case. A scan already RUNNING is returned as before and not
  gated; the open QUEUED scan a run adopts is excluded from the count,
  because adopting it IS starting it.
- **`402 /problems/scan-limit-reached`** (`errors.ScanLimitReached`) with
  `code` `SCAN_LIMIT_FREE_USED` or `SCAN_LIMIT_MONTHLY`, `scansUsed`,
  `scanLimit`, and `periodResetsAt` (first instant of next month, UTC) for
  the monthly case. The free detail says "Subscribe"; the monthly detail
  names the reset date and offers no upgrade, because there is no tier
  above this one.
- **Failed-open when billing is not configured.** `gate_enabled` is both
  `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` and `STRIPE_PRICE_ID` set; otherwise the gate is off,
  matching checkout's `503 billing-not-configured`. Stated in the docstring.
  **This bit the suite first**: `conftest.py` supplied placeholder Stripe
  keys "so point-of-use checks pass", which put every second scan in the
  suite behind a 402 — 28 failures across nine files on the first full run.
  The suite's default settings now leave both unset, which is the world CI
  and local development actually live in; `test_billing.py` and the new
  `test_scan_allowance.py` set the keys per test.
- **`GET /agencies/{id}/billing`** gains `scansUsedThisPeriod`, `scanLimit`
  (null when no gate applies) and `periodResetsAt` (null for free). One
  COUNT, no Stripe call. OpenAPI and `api.gen.ts` regenerated and confirmed
  stable on a second regeneration.
- **Prompt re-runs are not scans**: they create no `Scan` row and stay
  under the 30-an-hour throttle, which is unchanged. A test proves two
  re-runs after a 402 succeed and move the count by nothing.
- **Grandfathered: nobody.** Existing completed scans count, so every
  agency that has scanned is at "free scan used", the founder's included.

## Built — web

- `lib/billing/allowance.ts`: the label — "1 free scan" / "Free scan used" /
  "12 of 40 scans this month" / "40 of 40 scans this month · resets 1 Oct
  2026" — built only from the billing response, and `scanLimitProblem`,
  which narrows a 402. `useScanAllowance(agencyId)` reads billing once; a
  member's 403 resolves to no label, the settings page's own degradation.
- `components/billing/ScanLimitNotice.tsx`: the 402 on screen. Free: one
  sentence and a **Subscribe** button into the existing Checkout. Monthly:
  the reset date and nothing to click. Never an `ErrorState`.
- The dashboard's Re-run and the intake result's "Run a scan" both show the
  label and both render the notice on a 402 instead of the error state.
- **Copy.** Pricing card: "40 scans a month. Viewing, sharing and exporting
  reports is never limited." and "Signing up is free and includes one full
  scan and report. Subscribe to keep scanning." Landing hero: "Your first
  scan is free. $160/month after that." The "not metered or capped" bullet
  is gone from the honest-limits list. Settings' billing lead and the
  panel's no-subscription, cancelled and unknown-status sentences no longer
  claim nothing is behind the plan. **The card's "40" is the one hand-typed
  copy of the number on the web**, by decision: a signed-out visitor has no
  billing response to read from. Everything signed-in reads the API.

## What goes live on push

Render deploys before CI finishes. The gate turns on there **only if
Render's `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` and `STRIPE_PRICE_ID` are both set** — the
2026-09-23 entry records that Render's Price variable was still the $29
one and had to be changed by hand. If both are set, the founder's own
organisation reads "Free scan used" on the next visit and subscribes
through Stripe test mode like anyone else. If either is unset, nothing is
gated in production yet and the card's copy is ahead of the deployment.

## Verified

API **1457/1457** on a solo run (a wall-clock bound in `test_call_bounds`
failed once while three suites shared the machine, and passed three times
alone; +28 allowance tests: the constants argued, free 0→1→402, failed and

- **`Settings.scan_allowance_exempt_emails`**, default

# Two holes in the scan allowance: stranded scans, and an exemption on an unverified string

**2026-09-28.** The gate shipped earlier the same day. Two ways it refuses
the wrong person, both closed here.

## The measurement first

`avp_dev`: **27 scans across 6 agencies — 14 `partial`, 12 `succeeded`, 1
`failed`. Zero QUEUED and zero RUNNING**, stranded or otherwise. So the
count per agency is zero for all six, and the local database shows the
defect not at all. That is expected rather than reassuring: local scans run
through `InlineScanExecutor` or `scripts/verify_e2e.py`, both of which drive
a scan to a terminal status in-process, and nothing here restarts a web
process mid-queue. The defect is a property of the deployed executor, not of
the data.

**Production was not measured: the repository holds no credential that
reaches it.** `apps/api/.env` points at a local 5432 server; the Render
Postgres URL lives only in Render's own environment. The two deployed hosts
recorded on 2026-09-22 are the API and web services, not the database. The
count there is therefore unknown, and this entry does not guess it. What can
be said without the data: every Render deploy restarts the API process, a
deploy happens on every push, and this repository has pushed 5 commits today
alone — so any scan queued in those windows was stranded by construction.

## 1. A stranded QUEUED or RUNNING scan no longer holds a slot forever

`COUNTED_STATUSES` counted QUEUED and RUNNING unconditionally. Counting them
is right — it is what makes the row lock mean anything, and without it two
requests at the cap both see room. Counting them *forever* was the bug, and
there are two ways a scan reaches that state and stays:

- **Lost executor.** The executor is a per-request `BackgroundTasks` job and
  Render restarts on every deploy. A scan queued seconds before a restart is
  never picked up.
- **Detection-only scans.** Epic 3's competitor detection leaves an open
  QUEUED row for a later run to adopt (`get_or_create_scan`), which is
  deliberate and correct. But a free agency that ran detection on client A
  and then started a scan on client B was counted for A's row and refused
  `SCAN_LIMIT_FREE_USED` with no scan ever having run.

Either way the one free scan was burned by a scan that produced nothing,
which is precisely the rule the gate was built on — a failure never burns
the allowance.

**Now:** SUCCEEDED and PARTIAL count for good; QUEUED and RUNNING count only
while `created_at` is within `IN_FLIGHT_WINDOW = timedelta(minutes=15)`.
Fifteen minutes is three times the 300-second scan budget, the one duration
this product commits to. Three times rather than one so a slow but live scan
is never written off mid-flight — and the margin is real rather than
nominal, because that budget is currently **missed**: north-star.md records
the best measured run at 361.3s, so the window is still ~2.5x the slowest
scan actually observed. The race protection is untouched: two requests
contending for the last slot arrive milliseconds apart, deep inside the
window.

## Separate finding, not fixed here: QUEUED rows are never reaped

`reap_stale_scans` is **RUNNING-only, and deliberately so** — its docstring
says QUEUED means "open, nobody has claimed it", which is the state
detect-now-scan-tomorrow depends on. It also reaps only RUNNING rows that
hold a non-NULL expired lease, so a scan driven straight through
`scan_runner.run_scan` (the verify scripts, `conftest.py`) is never reaped
either. **Nothing in this system ever clears a stranded QUEUED row.** The
reaper was left alone as the brief directed; the 15-minute window makes the
allowance correct regardless of whether such a row is ever cleaned up, but
the row itself still sits there, and `get_or_create_scan` will still adopt
it however old it is. Worth its own pass.

## 2. The operator exemption now requires a Google-verified identity

`is_exempt` matched `User.email`, a string. **Password sign-up never
verifies that address**: `services/auth.sign_up_agency` hashes a password
and writes the user `ACTIVE` in one transaction, there is no confirmation
step anywhere in the flow, and there is no `email_verified` column on
`User` at all. So on any database where the founder's row does not already
exist — a new environment, a restore, a deleted account — the first person
to sign up by password with that address would have been handed unlimited
scans at about $1.70 each. Today's production row happens to be the
founder's, which is luck, not a control.

**Now:** exempt requires the listed address **and** a non-NULL
`User.google_sub`. That column is written only by `services/google_oauth`,
against a token Google signed, so it is the one fact here that an outside
party has vouched for. A password-only account on a listed address is gated
like everyone else. The Google-link path is covered by the same condition:
`google_sub` is unique, and it is set either by a Google-created account or
by linking an existing account through its Google-verified email, so the
exemption cannot be reached by anyone Google has not vouched for.

**The address is out of the code.** `Settings.scan_allowance_exempt_emails`
now defaults to `[]` — a personal address does not belong in source, and an
empty default means a fresh deployment exempts nobody until someone decides
otherwise. `.env.example` leaves the value empty. The live value belongs in
`SCAN_ALLOWANCE_EXEMPT_EMAILS` on the **Render API service**; until it is
set there, the founder is gated like any other user.

`is_exempt`, `allowance` and `assert_can_start` now take the `User` row
rather than an email string, because the question is about the account and
not about one of its columns. Both call sites already had `principal.user`
in hand.

inside-the-window tests pass — the new tests measure the new behaviour.

# The free scan requires a verified identity

**2026-09-29.** The finding of 2026-09-28, acted on: password sign-up never
verifies an address, the free scan is per agency, and an agency costs
nothing to make. Sign up with any string, take one scan (about $1.70 of
engine calls and 6 of SerpApi's 250 searches a month), repeat — about 41
fake sign-ups spend SerpApi's month, and competitor detection then stops for
every customer at once. The landing page says "Your first scan is free" in
public. The decision was made in the brief and is not reopened here: **the
free scan runs only for a requesting user with a linked Google identity**
(`User.google_sub` not null) — the one verified identity fact the system
already holds, the same basis as the operator exemption, and no new
infrastructure. Email verification (Resend plus a confirmation flow) stays
a later decision.

## The way through, confirmed before relying on it

Read, then run. `/auth/google/start` takes no session. The callback's
`resolve_identity` matches by `sub`, then by email; a password account with
no `google_sub` is linked when Google says `email_verified` and the account
is active and not deleted; the callback commits, replaces the cookie and
sends the browser to `/dashboard`. The existing
`test_a_password_account_links_by_verified_email_and_signs_in` covers the
brief's order (sign out, then Continue with Google). A new test drives the
notice's own order — still signed in: 402 `SCAN_LIMIT_VERIFY_REQUIRED` →
`/auth/google/start` → callback → `/dashboard` → the same scan 202, same
agency, `signInMethods` `["email", "google"]`. Google itself is faked at
the provider seam, as in every Google test here; the real consent screen
still needs the founder's account. Nothing else was needed, so no linking
flow was built.

**Gap found, not fixed.** When the Google attempt fails while the person is
still signed in — Cancel on Google's screen, or an address already linked to
another Google account — the callback sends them to `/?google=error&reason=…`
with their session still live. `app/page.tsx` resolves the session first and
shows the failure sentence only on the sign-in view, so it is dropped and
they land on intake with no word said. Signed out first, the sentence shows.
It is not something linking needs, so it is left for its own pass.

## Built — API

- **`services/scan_allowance.py`.** `has_verified_identity(user)` —
  `google_sub` set — is now what both the free scan and the operator
  exemption rest on. `Allowance.free_scan_requires_google` is true exactly
  when the gate is on, the agency is free and the requesting user has no
  link; `assert_can_start` raises `ScanLimitReached` with
  `SCAN_LIMIT_VERIFY_REQUIRED` on it (`scansUsed`, `scanLimit: 1`,
  `periodResetsAt: null`), **under the same row lock, before the count is
  consulted**, and no scan row is created. `user` is now a required argument
  of `allowance` and `assert_can_start`: an allowance is always somebody's.
- **Before the count, as the brief directed, and for a reason worth keeping.**
  The count is not a record of scans actually run: a detection-only QUEUED
  row holds a slot for its 15-minute window, so a password-only agency that
  never scanned would otherwise hear "your free scan is used". **Accepted
  consequence, pinned by a test:** where the free scan really is spent, a
  password-only user is asked for Google first and hears the scan is used
  only once linked. For a listed operator address signed in by password,
  asking for Google first is exactly right — the link is what makes it
  exempt.
- **Per requesting user, not per agency.** A password-only teammate in a
  free agency whose owner is Google-linked is refused; the owner is not.
  Paid agencies are untouched (a payment is identity enough; forty a month
  for any seat), and so are exempt operators, who have a `google_sub` by
  definition, and any deployment where billing is not configured.
- **One Google account, one free scan** — written into the module docstring
  as the reason this closes the farm rather than raising its price.
  `google_sub` is UNIQUE and a user belongs to one agency; the only thing
  that ever clears it, re-issuing a seat's invitation, leaves the row and
  its unique address in the same agency. The one route around it, checked
  and recorded rather than claimed away: unlink a seat, then change that
  Google account's own address to a new one Google verifies — an inbox per
  scan, the price email verification would have charged.
- **`GET /agencies/{id}/billing` gains `freeScanRequiresGoogle`**, from the
  same `Allowance` the refusal reads, so the screen and the 402 cannot
  disagree. OpenAPI and `api.gen.ts` regenerated, and stable on a second
  regeneration. api-contracts.md carries the code, the field and an example
  body — and its stale "default: the founder's address" line for the
  exemption now says empty-by-default plus Google, which 2026-09-28 changed
  in code but not there.

## Built — web

- **Label** (`lib/billing/allowance.ts`): "Free scan needs Google sign-in"
  when `freeScanRequiresGoogle` is true, read before the count as the API
  checks it, so the label says what pressing the button will meet. The web
  works nothing out itself. The 402 narrowing knows the third code.
- **`ScanLimitNotice`**: "Your free scan needs a Google sign-in, so we know
  one person gets one. Continue with Google using this address, or
  subscribe." **Continue with Google** is the sign-in page's own
  `GoogleSignInButton` → `/auth/google/start`; **Subscribe** is the same
  Checkout, as the secondary button so the paid way on does not outshout
  the free one. Not an `ErrorState`.
- **Copy — four places made the unconditional claim**, not the two the brief
  named, because the pricing card worded it differently from the hero:
  the landing hero ("Your first scan is free with a Google sign-in.
  $160/month after that."); the pricing card ("Signing up is free. Your
  first scan is free with a Google sign-in. Subscribe to keep scanning.",
  was "Signing up is free and includes one full scan and report"); Settings'
  billing lead; and the billing panel's no-subscription sentence ("Your
  agency's first scan is free with a Google sign-in", was "Your agency has
  one free scan"). Every test that pinned an old string moved with it.
- Seen, not only asserted: rendered to static HTML with compiled CSS, both
  themes, 1280 and 390 wide. One row of buttons at 390 with no horizontal
  scroll; the Google button is its guideline 40px beside a 32px secondary
  Subscribe, centred. `docs/screenshots/free-scan-google-2026-09-29/`.

## What goes live on push

Render deploys before CI finishes. Where the gate is on (both Stripe
variables set on Render), every password-only user of a free agency now
reads "Free scan needs Google sign-in" and meets the notice. **This leans on
Google sign-in being configured on Render** — the three `GOOGLE_OAUTH_*`
variables, recorded as set on 2026-09-22. Without them Continue with Google
is a 503 and a password-only free user's only way on is Subscribe.

# A failed Google step is explained to someone still signed in, and the workers lock is current

**2026-09-29, later the same day.** Two things the free-scan pass left
behind. The first was recorded there as a minor gap, and it no longer is:
the `SCAN_LIMIT_VERIFY_REQUIRED` notice sends a **signed-in** user to
`/auth/google/start`, which is exactly the path where a failure was dropped
without a word. The second is the workers lockfile, which that pass left
uncommitted as not its business.

## 1. The front door speaks to someone still signed in

**Before.** `app/page.tsx` read the failure reason before the session check
but showed it only on the sign-in view. Someone who pressed Cancel on
Google's screen, or picked a Google account whose address belongs to
another account here, came back signed in and landed on intake with nothing
said. Run a scan then met the same notice again, in a loop, with no
explanation.

**Now.** `lib/auth/googleFailure.takeGoogleFailure` reads the reason word
and clears the query first, so a reload does not repeat it. After the
session check:

- **Signed in:** the same `ErrorState`, "Google sign-in did not complete",
  above the intake form, in words written for someone signed in.
- **Signed out:** unchanged — the sign-in view with the sign-in page's own
  words.

**The sentences, checked for a reader who is already signed in.** Eight of
the ten were written for someone signing in: "sign in with your email and
password", "start it again from this page", "contact the agency's owner",
"cannot be used to sign in here", an invitation to accept. Those eight now
have signed-in variants in `GOOGLE_REASONS_SIGNED_IN`. `denied` and `exchange-failed` read true for
both and keep one sentence.

A live session proves the reader's own account is active and not deleted
(`current_principal` refuses anything else). So `email-claimed`,
`account-suspended`, `invitation-expired` and `account-unavailable` are
always about the account at the chosen Google account's address, which is
somebody else's row. The way out is the same for all four, and each variant
names this sign-in's own address:

> The address on the Google account you chose already belongs to another
> account here, so nothing was linked. Continue with Google again and choose
> dana@northlight.example.

## 2. A different Google address starts a new agency, and the notice now says so

**Checked, not assumed.** `resolve_identity` looks for a user by `sub`, then
by email. For a Google account whose address and `sub` are both unknown
here, it finds nobody and returns no user. The callback then treats it as a
brand-new sign-up: it mints a ticket and sends the browser to
`/sign-up/google` to name an agency.

- So a signed-in password user who picks the wrong Google account is not
  linked and not refused. They are walked into creating a second agency.
- Nothing is linked and their session is untouched until they finish that
  form. If they do, a new agency exists with its own free scan, and the
  cookie moves to it.
- A new test pins this. `/sign-up/google` was not changed: it does not know
  the person is still signed in elsewhere, but it does show the other
  address, which is their second chance to notice.

**"Using this address" was not enough.** The notice never shows an address,
and Google's account chooser lists every account signed into the browser.
The notice now reads:

> Your free scan needs a Google sign-in, so we know one person gets one.
> Continue with Google using the same address you sign in with here, or
> subscribe. A different Google account would start a new agency instead.

The API's `detail` for the same code says "the same address you sign in
with here" too. The notice does not print the literal address, because the
dashboard's payload carries no user; that would need an extra `/auth/me` or
a new member on the 402. The failure sentences on `/` do name it, since that
page already has `me`.

## 3. The workers lock is current, and CI checks both

**The drift, demonstrated.**
- The committed `apps/workers/uv.lock` held no `pyjwt` at all, although
  `avp-api` has required `pyjwt[crypto]` since Epic 20.
- `uv lock --check` failed on it (rc 1).
- A fresh environment built from it exactly as CI builds one
  (`uv sync --frozen --extra dev`) could not
  `import avp_api.services.google_oauth`, nor even `import avp_api.main`:
  `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'jwt'`.
- The workers suite stayed green only because nothing in it imports either.

**Re-locked.** `uv lock` added `pyjwt` and `cryptography`, and nothing else
moved. It picked `pyjwt` 2.15.1, released the day before. The two locks
share 65 packages, and every one of the other 64 was pinned identically in
both. So the new pin was held at the api's 2.13.0
(`uv lock --upgrade-package pyjwt==2.13.0`), which is the version the API's
own suite tests its Google code against.

- The diff is 53 added lines and no removals.
- `uv lock --check` passes.
- A fresh frozen environment imports both modules on `jwt` 2.13.0.
- The api lock passed `uv lock --check` as committed, so it was not
  re-locked.

**CI.** A `uv.lock is current` step (`uv lock --check`) now runs in both the
api and workers jobs, after `setup-uv` and before the frozen install. A
stale lock now fails CI instead of sitting as a local diff. The workers step
says why it matters there in particular: the API is a path dependency, so
the API's own `pyproject.toml` is an input to the workers lock.
